excerpt_integrity_check.method: Each evidence quote was matched exactly against the frozen summary and checked to begin and end on source line boundaries; full paragraphs and complete list items were selected. All checks passed.

clauses: Alien selection
Flare inclusion
Hand size
First player
answers.answer: Each player receives two flares and their matching alien sheets, secretly chooses one alien, and returns the other sheet. Both flares dealt to every player—including flares for rejected aliens—enter the cosmic deck; add random extras if needed to reach ten flares. Deal eight cards to each player. Draw destiny until a player color appears; that player starts, and the drawn card is shuffled back into the destiny deck.

evidence.heading: Setup
evidence.quote: 3. Shuffle the flares, deal two to each player, and give them the matching alien sheets. Each secretly chooses one alien, initially placing it facedown, and returns the other sheet to the box. This is the standard selection procedure; Hidden Powers is a separate excluded variant. The original text does not specify when standard-game sheets are turned faceup; unlike the optional Hidden Powers rule, it gives no explicit reveal window. This source gap is recorded rather than supplying a new setup rule. Green/yellow/red indicate recommended experience, not strength. Beginners may start with green aliens without flares.

evidence.heading: Setup
evidence.quote: 4. Add **both flares dealt to every player**, including rejected aliens' flares, to the cosmic deck. Add random extras if needed to reach ten flares total; shuffle. Deal eight-card hands. Keep card faces private unless an effect allows showing them.

evidence.heading: Setup
evidence.quote: 5. Draw destiny until a player color appears; that player starts. Shuffle the drawn card back into the destiny deck. Play passes left thereafter.

clauses: Definition of one colony
Coexistence of several players’ colonies on one planet
Whether five foreign colonies must be in different systems
answers.answer: One or more ships of a color on a planet form that color’s one colony; adding ships does not create more colonies. Different colors can each have a colony on the same planet. Five foreign colonies may all be in one other system.

evidence.heading: Overview
evidence.quote: Each player leads an alien trying to establish five **foreign colonies**. A colony is one or more ships of one color on one planet; extra ships on that planet do not make extra colonies. Several colors can coexist there, each with its own colony. Home colonies are in your own system; foreign colonies are outside it. Five foreign planets can all be in one other system. Alien powers override conflicting general rules.

clauses: Whether offense must retrieve a warp ship if available
Where it goes if offense has colonies
Where it goes if offense has none
answers.answer: At Regroup, offense must retrieve one of its ships from the warp if any is available. It goes to an existing home or foreign colony. If offense has no colonies, the original rulebook puts it directly in the gate. The summary also records an FAQ exception: a player with no colonies or ships on their turn may instead place it on any home planet.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure — Regroup
evidence.quote: Offense must retrieve one of its ships from the warp if available, placing it on any existing home or foreign colony. The original rulebook puts this retrieved ship directly in the gate if offense has no colonies. The FAQ adds that a player who has no colonies or ships on their turn may instead place the Regroup ship on any home planet. Ordinary relocation with no colony to receive ships sends them to the warp; the stated Regroup exceptions take precedence.

clauses: Handling destiny when one card remains
Own-color choices when a foreign colony is in own home system
Own-color choice when there is a completely empty home planet
answers.answer: If one destiny card remains, do not draw it: shuffle it with the destiny discards and draw from the new deck. On own color, offense may redraw or choose a foreign colony in its home system; that colony’s owner defends and other colonies are bystanders. Alternatively it can choose a home planet with no ships of any color and move up to four ships there from other colonies, reclaiming it automatically as a win/successful encounter.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure — Destiny
evidence.quote: Draw destiny to determine the defense and target system. **When only one card remains, do not draw it**: shuffle it with the destiny discards, then draw from the new deck.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure — Destiny
evidence.quote: - Your own color: redraw, or target one chosen foreign colony in your home system, making its owner the defense. Other colonies there are bystanders. You can instead aim at a home planet with **no ships of any color**, moving up to four ships from other colonies there to reclaim it automatically. This counts as a win and successful encounter, proceeds only through Launch, and can qualify you for a second encounter.

clauses: Whether offense may attack Blue’s foreign colony in Red’s home system after drawing Blue
Who defends Red’s empty home planet if foreign bystanders are present
answers.answer: Without a special power, no: drawing Blue targets Blue in Blue’s home system, and an ordinary color destiny does not allow attacking Blue’s colony in Red’s system. Red defends Red’s empty home planet because the home-system owner defends even with zero ships there; foreign colonies present are bystanders and are unaffected by the encounter.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure — Destiny
evidence.quote: - Another player's color: encounter that player in their home system.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure — Destiny
evidence.quote: Destiny hazard symbols have no effect in this base game. Ordinarily you cannot attack a player's foreign colony in a third player's system: a color/wild/special targets its defense in that player's home system, while your own color permits driving out a foreign colony in your own system. If you already have colonies on **all planets in the defensive system**, draw destiny again.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure — Launch
evidence.quote: Defense cannot add or subtract ships on the target. The owner of a home system defends their planet even with zero ships there. Other colors' colonies are **bystanders**: they add nothing to the defense and the encounter result does not harm them. When driving out a foreign colony, target only that one color's colony; all other colors are bystanders.

clauses: Source and number of offense ships
Whether offense may strip a colony
Defense movement during Launch
answers.answer: Offense launches one to four ships from any combination of its existing home and foreign colonies and may strip a colony; removing its last ship immediately eliminates that colony. Defense cannot add or subtract ships on the target during Launch.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure — Launch
evidence.quote: Aim the gate at one planet in the indicated system; put one to four of your ships in it, drawn from any combination of your existing home and foreign colonies. You may strip a colony, but removing its last ship immediately eliminates it. Ships returning from an encounter or warp cannot return to that now-empty location as though it remained your colony.

clauses: Order of ally invitations and commitments
Whether a player invited by both sides may join both
Location for defensive ally ships
answers.answer: Offense invites first, then defense; after invitations, each other player in clockwise order starting left of offense accepts one invitation or declines and commits ships before the next player decides. A player may join only one side or neither. Defensive allies put ships beside the target planet, not on it.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure — Alliance
evidence.quote: Offense names invited allies first; they wait to answer. Defense then invites allies, possibly including the same players. Neither main player may invite the other. Starting with the player left of offense and proceeding clockwise, each other player accepts one invitation or declines all, then commits ships before the next player decides. You may join only one side or neither; normally an invitation is required.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure — Alliance
evidence.quote: Each ally contributes one to four ships from any of their colonies. Offensive allies place them on the gate; defensive allies place them beside the target planet, **not on it**. The FAQ nevertheless considers defensive allies in the gate for effects referring to that location. Parasite changes invitation eligibility.

clauses: Winner from the totals
Disposition of offense ships
Disposition of offensive ally ships
Disposition of defense ships
Disposition of defensive ally ships and reward
Bystander result
answers.answer: Totals tie: offense is 10 + 6 = 16 and defense is 12 + 4 = 16, so defense wins ties. Offense and its offensive allies go to the warp. The defending main player’s ships and bystander colonies stay. The four defensive ships remain with the defensive side; its ally’s three committed ships return to any of that ally’s own colonies. The defensive ally earns three rewards, each independently chosen as one cosmic-deck draw or one own warp ship retrieved to any own colony; choices can be combined. Bystanders are unharmed.

evidence.heading: Attack against attack
evidence.quote: Each side's total is its main player's attack value plus all ships on its side: offense and offensive allies in the gate; defense on the target plus defensive allies beside it. Higher total wins; **defense wins ties**. Powers and played cards may change this calculation or the winner.

evidence.heading: Attack against attack — Defense wins
evidence.quote: - **Defense wins:** defending and bystander colonies stay. Offense and offensive allies go to warp. Defensive allies return their committed ships to any existing own colonies, even different origins; helping defend does not grant a colony on the defended planet. Each defensive ally also receives **one defender reward per ship contributed**. For each reward, draw one cosmic-deck card or retrieve one own warp ship to any own colony; combine these choices freely.

clauses: Destinations of ships on each side when offense wins
Whether bystander colonies survive
Whether reinforcing an existing colony grants another colony
answers.answer: All offense and offensive-ally ships land on the target; defense and defensive-ally ships go to the warp. Existing bystander colonies survive. Reinforcing a colony already established there does not advance the colony marker or count as another colony.

evidence.heading: Attack against attack — Offense wins
evidence.quote: - **Offense wins:** all offense and offensive ally ships land on the target, establishing or reinforcing each color's colony. Defense and defensive ally ships go to warp. Bystanders survive. Advance a colony marker only for a newly established foreign colony, not reinforcement of an existing colony.

clauses: Whether defensive ally may combine rewards
Reward choices per each of three contributed ships
Destinations of the ally’s ships and retrieved ships
answers.answer: Yes. Three contributed defensive ships earn three separate rewards, and the ally may mix deck draws and warp retrievals among them. Their committed ships return to any of their existing colonies. Each retrieved warp ship goes to any own colony chosen for that reward.

evidence.heading: Attack against attack — Defense wins
evidence.quote: - **Defense wins:** defending and bystander colonies stay. Offense and offensive allies go to warp. Defensive allies return their committed ships to any existing own colonies, even different origins; helping defend does not grant a colony on the defended planet. Each defensive ally also receives **one defender reward per ship contributed**. For each reward, draw one cosmic-deck card or retrieve one own warp ship to any own colony; combine these choices freely.

clauses: Compensation amount for main player losing negotiate to attack
Source of compensation
Treatment of two allied ships also sent to warp
If opponent has fewer cards
answers.answer: The losing main player takes one random card from the opponent’s hand per own ship actually lost to the warp: three cards here. The two allied losses do not count, and allies receive no compensation. If the opponent has fewer than the required cards, take the entire hand. Cards are taken unseen from the opponent’s hand.

evidence.heading: Attack against negotiate: compensation
evidence.quote: The negotiate player automatically loses; resolve the winner's ship destinations normally. The losing main player randomly takes one card from the opponent's hand for each of **their own ships actually lost to the warp**. Exclude allied losses: allies receive no compensation. If the opponent lacks sufficient cards, take the entire hand. Cards are taken without seeing their faces. Compensation is stolen hand cards; defender rewards are deck draws and/or warp retrieval.

clauses: Allies’ outcome and deal participation
Time limit and exchange options for main players
Where a colony may be granted
Validity of a deal
Failure penalty and time limit
answers.answer: Both sides’ allies return their ships to their own colonies, gain nothing, and cannot join the deal. The main players have one minute to exchange hand cards and/or grant each other one colony on a planet where the giver already has a colony (including a foreign colony); the recipient can use any own ships not in the warp. A valid deal actually transfers at least one card or colony, and may be one-sided; doing nothing is invalid. Card promises must be truthful and honored; future promises are unenforceable. If no agreement is reached within one minute, each main player loses three ships of their choice to the warp, and offense cannot take an ordinary second encounter.

evidence.heading: Negotiate against negotiate: making a deal
evidence.quote: Both sides' allies return ships to their own colonies, gain nothing and cannot participate in the deal. The main players have **one minute**. They may transfer cards from their hands and/or each grant the other **one colony on a planet where the giver already has a colony**, including a foreign colony. The recipient can use any own ships not in the warp. Existing ships coexist; the giver need not vacate, and vacating would eliminate the colony being offered. Return any remaining gate ships to offense's colonies.

evidence.heading: Negotiate against negotiate: making a deal
evidence.quote: A successful deal must actually transfer at least one card or colony; it may be one-sided. You cannot agree to do nothing. Tangible terms are restricted to permitted cards/colonies and specific power/card exceptions such as Zombie's liberation; future promises are unenforceable. Card terms may be explicit or vague but must be truthful and honored (if you promise your highest attack, give it). If time expires without agreement, **each main player loses three ships of their choice to the warp**, and offense cannot take an ordinary second encounter. Successful deals qualify for an ordinary second encounter but do not trigger win-only powers.

clauses: What Morph copies and when
Whether it tracks later changes to opponent’s card
What happens after encounter
answers.answer: Morph becomes an exact copy of the opponent’s initially revealed encounter card, including the initial attack value. Later modifications to the opponent’s card do not automatically apply to Morph; it may be modified separately. After the encounter, Morph returns to its normal identity.

evidence.heading: Morph
evidence.quote: The single base Morph becomes an exact copy of the opponent's initially revealed encounter card: attack copies its initial value, negotiate becomes negotiate. Resolve that pairing normally. Subsequent modifications of the opponent's card do not automatically carry over to Morph; Morph can be modified separately. For example, Tripler revealing Morph against attack12 copies12 and divides its own copy to4; Tripler revealing12 against Morph changes its own12 to4, while opponent's Morph remains12. Morph returns to its normal identity after the encounter. If two Morphs could be played against each other, both sides would lose all involved ships to warp; there is only one in this base deck.

clauses: Eligible reinforcement players
Timing
Which side they may reinforce
When response window ends
answers.answer: During Reveal, after encounter cards are revealed, either main player or any ally may play reinforcements to either side’s total, including the opposing side. Players may continue responding with reinforcements until all pass; then resolve with the updated totals. Bystanders cannot play them merely because they are present.

evidence.heading: Artifacts and reinforcements
evidence.quote: Reinforcements are not encounter cards. During Reveal, after encounter cards are revealed, either main player and any ally may play them to add to **either side's total**, including the opposing side. Players may respond with further reinforcements until all pass; then resolve using the new totals. Bystanders cannot play them merely because they are present on the planet.

clauses: Ordinary per-player flare limit
Per-card flare limit
When a flare returns to hand
Own Wild versus Super choice
answers.answer: A player may play at most one flare per encounter, and each particular flare may be used only once in that encounter even if it changes hands. A played flare returns to hand immediately after its effect finishes. If it is your alien’s flare and your power is available, you must use Super rather than Wild; if the power is lost or zapped, only Wild is available.

evidence.heading: Flare system
evidence.quote: Return a flare to hand **immediately after its effect finishes**, rather than discard it, unless its effect states otherwise. A player may play **at most one flare per encounter**, and an individual flare can be used **only once per encounter even if it changes hands**. A Card Zap targeting the flare counts against the player's limit. Prevention of play differs from cancellation after play: see Anti-Matter's FAQ exception. If a Super enables a power use, that power can still be Cosmic Zapped even outside its usual role/phase. The flare remains in hand rather than being discarded or forced to Wild; Wild becomes available while the power is zapped. When your own Wild would otherwise be handed to your alien, keep it after resolution.

evidence.heading: Flare system
evidence.quote: Flares are not encounter cards. Each has printed Wild and Super effects, usage roles and timing. Normally use Wild; if it is your own alien's flare and your power is available, **you must use Super**, not choose Wild. If your power is lost or zapped, you can use only Wild until your power returns.

clauses: Offense with no encounter cards at start of turn
Defense with no encounter cards at Planning
Offense losing its last encounter card later
Whether non-encounter cards must be played before replacement
answers.answer: At Start Turn before Regroup, an offense without encounter cards reveals and discards its remaining hand, then draws eight cards. At defense’s Planning, if it lacks encounter cards it reveals/discards its remainder and draws eight, repeating until it has an encounter card. If offense runs out later when it needs to play an encounter card, its turn ends rather than replacing the hand; offense and allies return committed ships to offense’s colonies, with the normal no-colony relocation rule. Playing legally playable non-encounter cards before the start-turn replacement is optional, not compulsory.

evidence.heading: Start Turn and hand replacement
evidence.quote: Start Turn occurs only before the first encounter of your turn, before Regroup effects. If offense has no encounter cards, reveal and discard the remaining hand, then draw eight new cards. You may first play legally playable non-encounter cards but are not required to play them. Hate draws a needed starting hand before using its power.

evidence.heading: Start Turn and hand replacement
evidence.quote: At Planning, a defense lacking encounter cards reveals/discards the remainder and draws eight cards, repeating until it has an encounter card. An offense that runs out later in its turn **when it needs to play an encounter card** ends its turn instead of drawing a replacement: offense and all allies return committed ships to any of their own colonies. The normal no-colony relocation rule applies. There is no automatic draw at the end of an encounter or turn, or merely for running out of cards. Alien and card effects can grant different draws.

clauses: Whether offense can begin a second encounter without an encounter card in hand
What ends an ordinary turn after first or second encounter
answers.answer: No. A second encounter requires an encounter card already in offense’s hand; offense cannot begin one hoping to obtain a card later. Ordinarily, after an unsuccessful first encounter the turn passes left; after the second encounter the turn passes left. A successful first encounter permits an optional second encounter if the hand condition is met.

evidence.heading: Turn Structure
evidence.quote: The active player is the **offense**. Offense and defense are the **main players**. A turn normally has one encounter and, optionally, a second after a successful first encounter. Winning or making a successful deal is successful; making a deal is **not a win** for an effect that only says win. A second encounter requires at least one encounter card already in the offense's hand; you cannot start it hoping to obtain one before Planning. After the second encounter, or an unsuccessful first encounter, the turn passes left. Machine provides an exception.

clauses: Exact home-colony threshold and timing for loss/restoration
Whether power may be used once after falling below threshold
Scope of Cosmic Zap across printed sheet effects
answers.answer: Below three home colonies, the sheet is immediately turned facedown and the ordinary alien power is lost; there is no last use. It returns faceup once the player again occupies at least three home planets. Cosmic Zap cancels a power use and prevents further uses for that encounter; it does not stop printed clauses that do not require a power use.

evidence.heading: Power loss, zapping and timing
evidence.quote: With fewer than **three home colonies**, immediately turn your alien sheet facedown and lose its power; you cannot use it one last time. Restore it faceup when you again occupy at least three home planets. Masochist expressly keeps its power with fewer colonies. Losing a power also removes that alien identity for power-dependent effects and access to its Super.

evidence.heading: Power loss, zapping and timing
evidence.quote: A power may be Cosmic Zapped **only when being used**, not preemptively. The bold-italic **use** on an alien sheet identifies its cancellable use. Cancel that effect and prevent further uses until the encounter ends, including when zapped during Start Turn. Clauses that do not require use—such as Warrior adding experience, Zombie liberating ships in a deal, or placing a Citadel—are not themselves zappable uses. Zapping a use does not disable such clauses.

clauses: Order for contradictory simultaneous effects
Whether another non-Zap action can interrupt a resolving effect
Whether a power may be preemptively zapped
answers.answer: Resolve actual simultaneous contradictory effects in order: offense, defense, then other players clockwise starting left of offense. Finish one effect before starting another, except for a Zap or an effect expressly allowing interruption. A power cannot be preemptively Cosmic Zapped; it may be zapped only when it is being used.

evidence.heading: Power loss, zapping and timing
evidence.quote: Effects associated with no player resolve last, after the player order. Resolve actual simultaneous contradictory effects in order: **offense; defense; other players clockwise starting left of offense**. First honor more specific before/after timing within a phase. Finish one effect before starting another, except a Zap or an effect expressly allowing interruption. An optional effect's owner may change their mind when another effect or timing order changes the game state. Alien powers are normally usable once per relevant context, unless their text says otherwise.

clauses: Timing and sharing of ordinary five-colony victories
Outcome when Tick-Tock loses last token during a deal giving both main players their fifth foreign colony
answers.answer: Check ordinary five-foreign-colony wins at the very end of Resolution; players who meet the condition together share victory. If a deal gives both main players their fifth foreign colony and also removes Tick-Tock’s last token, all three share the win.

evidence.heading: Scoring / Victory Conditions
evidence.quote: Track **current** foreign colonies, decreasing the marker when one is lost. At the **very end of Resolution**, a player with five foreign colonies wins; multiple players meeting the condition together share victory. Other effects still have until that point to prevent ordinary victory. An effect explicitly saying immediately win ends the game when resolved, unless zapped or specifically interrupted. Masochist and Tick-Tock have printed alternate win conditions; Tick-Tock can share a deal-created win as described in its entry.

evidence.heading: Tick-Tock
evidence.quote:
#### Tick-Tock

**Patience — As any player; mandatory; Resolution.**

- Setup: Place ten tokens on sheet.
- Each time any player wins as defense OR successful deal made between any two players, discard one token from sheet.
- If no tokens left on sheet immediately win game. May also win normally.

**FAQ p21:** If a deal gives both main players their fifth foreign colony and removes your last token, all three share the win.
